name: Cuba
summary_text: Cuba is workable for trans visitors — one of Latin America's most legally transformed countries. The 2019 Constitution bans discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity; the 2022 Family Code (66.87% referendum approval) overhauled family law; and trans people can change legal gender — the July 2025 civil-registry reform further eliminated bureaucratic hurdles for name changes. CENESEX, the state sex-education centre, runs an official trans-care programme, and Havana has a visible, state-tolerated trans community. The counterweights are systemic rather than trans-specific: Cuba is a one-party state with no independent civil society, arbitrary-detention powers are broad, the economic crisis has degraded healthcare (hormone availability is unreliable), and police discretion is wide. There is no documented pattern of police targeting trans people as trans — the historical UMAP camps era is long past and officially repudiated — but there is also no independent recourse if something goes wrong. For a visitor: no legal exposure for gender expression or documents; low street-hostility in tourist areas; the risk is the general absence of rule-of-law recourse.

sources.title: Cuba’s LGBT Rights: Laws, History, and Real-World Gaps - LegalClarity
sources.claim_summary: LegalClarity overview (May 2026): Cuba's transformation from one of the most repressive systems (UMAP forced-labour camps for gay men, 1965-68, with 'curing' experiments) to one of the most progressive legal frameworks - the 2019 Constitution bans SOGI discrimination, the 2022 Family Code legalised same-sex marriage and adoption, and trans people can change legal gender without surgery - but a meaningful gap remains between law and daily reality.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters report (June 2025) covers Cuba's trans community seeing 'glimmer of hope' in proposed legislation.
ILGA World Database jurisdiction page for Cuba: documents LGBTI-related legal frameworks — status of same-sex conduct, gender recognition and protections.

sources.title: Cuba’s Family Code Referendum Is Sparking Deep Debates
sources.claim_summary: Americas Quarterly (Sept 2022): Cuba's Family Code referendum (legalising same-sex marriage and adoption) sparked deep public debate amid record emigration and another crackdown on dissent; community discussions showed both support and resistance.

Links International Journal of Socialist Renewal (Dec 2011): 'Rainbow Cuba: the sexual revolution within the revolution' - a sympathetic first-person account challenging the claim that Cuba is homophobic; includes a timeline from the 1939 anti-gay Social Defence Code through the UMAP camps (1965-68), the 1975 Supreme Court overturning of employment limits, the Family Code (1976), and CENESEX's work.

sources.title: Cuban lawmakers ban anti-gay employment discrimination
sources.claim_summary: Washington Blade (Dec 2013): Cuban lawmakers ban employment discrimination against gay workers.

sources.title: Cuban authorities not 'directly' targeting LGBTI asylum seeker's partner
sources.claim_summary: Washington Blade (May 2018): Cuban authorities say they are not 'directly' targeting the partner of an LGBTI asylum seeker.
